description:
We are a three member team brought together by an interest in space, technology, and building things. For Tenth Light, we wanted to make the process of designing a space mission something people could explore rather than just read about.

I (Ojus) handled the technical development, including the game's systems and implementation. Shreya created the demonstration presentation and contributed to research. Unnati helped with research and gathering project resources.
summary:
Tenth Light is a space mission design game that puts players in the role of a mission team. Starting in the Vehicle Assembly Building, players assemble a spacecraft, choose its systems, and work within engineering constraints before setting out on a journey through the Solar System.

The game turns topics such as spacecraft mass, power, propulsion, communications, launch capacity, and mission planning into decisions the player must make. Along the route, players encounter challenges involving the Moon, Ceres, Jupiter, Uranus, Neptune, and other destinations. Some stages use NASA data and imagery to connect gameplay to real space science.

The project also makes a distinction between established mission technology and speculative ideas. For example, JAXA’s IKAROS mission provides a real solar sail reference, while the interstellar journey is presented as an educational scenario rather than an existing capability.

Our aim is to make the choices behind space missions easier to explore. Instead of only reading about spacecraft engineering, players can experiment with trade offs and see how individual decisions affect a mission.
details:
What is Tenth Light?

Tenth Light is an educational space mission design game. It follows a mission from spacecraft assembly to a journey across the Solar System and, eventually, an imagined interstellar destination. Players take on the role of a mission team and make decisions that affect the spacecraft and its ability to complete the journey.

How the game works

1. Build the spacecraft

Players begin in the Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB). They choose spacecraft components and configure the vehicle while considering constraints such as mass, power, budget, propulsion, and mission requirements. The aim is to build a spacecraft that can support the planned journey.

2. Plan and fly the mission

The player follows a route through the Solar System. At different stops, they face interactive tasks and puzzles based on mission operations, navigation, communications, and planetary science.

3. Work through mission challenges

The journey includes challenges such as matching an antenna to calculated Earth pointing coordinates at the lunar station, navigating asteroid encounters, and solving destination specific puzzles. These stages turn technical ideas into actions the player must perform.

4. Explore real space data

NASA resources are used in several parts of the experience. The project queries the NASA Exoplanet Archive for TOI-700 system parameters, uses JPL Horizons calculations for the lunar antenna puzzle, and incorporates NASA NeoWs and DSCOVR EPIC data in the relevant mission views. NASA imagery is also used in the game's reconnaissance plates. When a live service is unavailable, some features use clearly documented fallback snapshots or curated values.

5. Reach the final destination

The story eventually introduces TOI-700 e and an imagined journey beyond the Solar System. The game uses this scenario to explore the scale of interstellar travel. Its 0.1c travel concept and 1,015 year journey are speculative educational elements, not a claim that current spacecraft can make this trip.

Why we made it

Space missions involve decisions that are difficult to understand when presented only as equations, diagrams, or technical reports. Tenth Light gives players a way to interact with those decisions. It is intended for students, space enthusiasts, and people who are curious about how missions are planned and operated.

What makes it different

The game connects spacecraft building decisions with a mission narrative. Players do not simply view space imagery or read facts; they use information and complete tasks as part of a connected journey. The project also identifies where it uses live data, offline snapshots, curated reference values, and speculative scenarios so that gameplay and scientific claims are not confused.

Tools and technologies

  • TypeScript and JavaScript: Application logic, game systems, and API integration.
  • Next.js and React: Web application structure, routing, and interactive interface.
  • Three.js: Real-time 3D spacecraft and assembly-bay visuals.
  • Tailwind CSS: Layout and styling.
  • NASA APIs and services: Exoplanet Archive, JPL Horizons, NeoWs, DSCOVR EPIC, NASA Image and Video Library, and JPL Photojournal.
  • Web Audio API: Procedurally generated interface sounds and ambience.
  • Playwright and Lighthouse: Browser testing and quality checks.
  • Vercel and GitHub: Hosting, deployment, and source-code management.

Limitations

Some external services may be unavailable during play, so the game includes offline fallback snapshots for selected features. The interstellar journey is fictional, and the game does not simulate a scientifically complete spacecraft or a real mission proposal. Some historical image credits and reuse terms also require individual review; the project does not claim that every NASA hosted image is automatically public domain.

SI Tools Disclosure: Antigravity (powered by Gemini) and Claude were used for research and information gathering, coding, debugging and troubleshooting, and presentation development.
